title: Responding to Incidents and Events
objective: Process events in context, implement changes with a limited scope of impact, and troubleshoot.

sections.title: Route Events Correctly to Notifications and Processing
paragraphs: For event-driven response, define the source, event format, matching conditions, duplicates, ordering, retries, and destination when processing fails. Even when receiving events from services such as AWS Health, EventBridge, and CloudTrail, do not send everything through the same automated process. Instead, separate notifications, tickets, investigations, and automation according to severity and impact.

When using fan-out, queues, or workflows, design idempotent processing and dead-letter handling on the assumption that delivery may occur at least once and that duplicates may occur. Discarding an event as a failure can result in missed responses and gaps in root-cause investigation.

sources.label: DOP-C02 Exam Guide: Responding to Incidents and Events

sections.title: Establishing Safety Boundaries for Automated Remediation
paragraphs: Implement automated responses to configuration drift and incidents as runbooks with a defined scope, prerequisites, execution permissions, concurrency limits, success criteria, stop conditions, and rollback procedures. Changing every environment without limiting the scope can turn false positives or temporary dependency failures into an outage affecting the entire environment.

After remediation, verify the change history and the same user-impact metrics. If there is no improvement, do not retry indefinitely; stop the execution, escalate, and hand off the hypotheses and evidence.

sections.title: Troubleshoot Incidents Using Evidence
paragraphs: Incident responders compare the time of occurrence, the affected operations and users, immediately preceding deployments and configuration changes, dependencies, request paths, logs, and metrics on a single timeline. They do not determine the cause based solely on a single CPU spike or one log entry.

Changes made for troubleshooting should limit the scope of impact and record the hypothesis, the expected change, the observed values, and how to roll back. Even when urgent recovery is needed, do not erase evidence or remove all protections.

checkpoints.prompt: A person responsible for running automated processing in response to infrastructure change events wants to prevent the same change from being applied twice when duplicate events occur. Select one most appropriate event-processing design.

choices.text: Process events idempotently using the event ID or target state, and design verification for retries and the dead-letter queue.
choices.explanation: This allows processing to remain safe even when duplicates or transient failures occur.

choices.text: Assume that each event is delivered only once, and discard it if processing fails.
choices.explanation: This can cause both missed responses and duplicate changes.

choices.text: Run every event unconditionally through the same administrator script.
choices.explanation: This cannot distinguish differences in priority or impact scope.

checkpoints.prompt: You want to prevent a runbook that automatically remediates configuration drift from affecting the entire production environment in the event of a false positive. Select one most appropriate runbook design.

choices.text: Define the targets, prerequisites, least-privilege permissions, concurrency limit, and success, stop, and rollback conditions, then run it in a limited scope.
choices.explanation: This lets you control the scope of the automation’s impact.

choices.text: Apply it immediately to all environments when detected, without defining stop conditions.
choices.explanation: This would expand a false positive into an incident affecting the entire environment.

choices.text: Do not check the metrics after remediation.
choices.explanation: You cannot verify the effectiveness or any secondary incidents.

checkpoints.prompt: Order failures have increased after a new deployment. Select one most appropriate initial diagnostic step for the incident responder.

choices.text: Restart all services because CPU utilization is high.
choices.explanation: This expands the impact without confirming the cause.

choices.text: Compare the affected operations, times, users, change history, request paths, dependencies, logs, and metrics on the same timeline.
choices.explanation: This allows you to test the relationship to the change as a hypothesis.

choices.text: Delete the logs to make the investigation easier.
